propositions.text: The appellant admitted unlawfully causing death and was guilty of manslaughter, but the jury convicted him of second degree murder.
propositions.quote: The appellant admitted that he unlawfully caused the death of the victim and was therefore guilty of manslaughter. The jury convicted on the charge of second degree murder.

propositions.text: The appeal concerns whether the trial judge erred in answering jury questions about manslaughter.
propositions.quote: This appeal as of right brought pursuant to s. 691(1) (a) of the Criminal Code... turns on whether the trial judge erred in his answer to questions from the jury about the offence of manslaughter

propositions.text: The dissent held the jury should have been told the actus reus was admitted and the mental element required intentional force and objective foreseeability of bodily harm.
propositions.quote: In this case, where the unlawful act had been admitted, it should have been explained to the jury that the actus reus had been admitted... the mental element of the offence... required both the intentional application of force... and the objective foreseeability of the risk of bodily harm

propositions.text: The trial judge did not err and the appeal should be dismissed, agreeing with the majority of the Alberta Court of Appeal.
propositions.quote: In my view, the trial judge did not err and for the reasons of the majority of the Alberta Court of Appeal... I would dismiss the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellant admitted manslaughter but was convicted of murder; the appeal concerns jury instructions on manslaughter; the dissent argued for clearer instructions; the court finds no error and would dismiss the appeal.

propositions.text: The trial judge responded helpfully and correctly to the jury's questions and encouraged further questions if needed.
propositions.quote: I would add only that the judge responded helpfully and correctly to the jury’s questions... the trial judge in this case encouraged the jury to pose a further question if his answer did not assist them.

propositions.text: The jury asked for layman terms difference between murder 2 and manslaughter and a specific definition of manslaughter.
propositions.quote: The jury asked: “In ‘layman terms’ what is the difference between murder 2 and manslaughter? Examples? . . . A specific definition of manslaughter?”

propositions.text: The judge explained the difference is in mental state, reviewed murder mental element, and said manslaughter applies if murder mental state not proved.
propositions.quote: the judge told the jury that the difference is in the accused’s mental state and then reviewed the portion of his original charge... if the appellant was not proved to have had the mental state required for murder, then the killing is manslaughter.

propositions.text: The judge declined to give examples fearing they would not clarify the difference and explained each case depends on its own facts.
propositions.quote: The judge declined to give the jury examples for fear that they would not make the difference between murder and manslaughter any clearer.

propositions.text: The judge said there is no specific definition of manslaughter in the Criminal Code but explained the jury's task and encouraged further questions.
propositions.quote: With respect to the jury’s inquiry about a “specific definition of manslaughter”, the judge told the jury that there is no specific definition of manslaughter in the Criminal Code... He concluded by encouraging the jury to formulate a further question if his answers did not assist them.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge responded helpfully to jury questions, explained mental state differences, declined examples, and encouraged further questions.

propositions.text: No legal error occurred in the instructions; no reasonable possibility the jury misunderstood murder or manslaughter elements.
propositions.quote: there is no legal error as contended by the appellant in these instructions. There is no reasonable possibility that the jury could have misunderstood what had to be proved...

propositions.text: Instructions focused the jury on the sole issue and gave correct legal principles for decision.
propositions.quote: The instructions focussed the jury on the sole issue it had to decide and gave them the correct legal principles necessary for them to do so.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no legal error in instructions and no reasonable possibility the jury misunderstood the issues or legal principles.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed.
propositions.quote: I would dismiss the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal.

propositions.text: The dissenting judges would allow the appeal and order a new trial for substantially the same reasons as the Court of Appeal dissent.
propositions.quote: Like O’Brien J.A., dissenting in the Court of Appeal... I would allow the appeal and order a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: The dissent would allow the appeal and order a new trial for similar reasons as the Court of Appeal dissent.

propositions.text: The trial judge directed the jury to convict either murder or manslaughter but gave no definition or instructions on manslaughter elements.
propositions.quote: the trial judge directed the jury that they were bound to convict the appellant of either murder or manslaughter. He directed the jury on the essential elements of murder but gave them no definition and no instructions at all on the essential elements of manslaughter.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge told the jury to convict murder or manslaughter but gave no manslaughter definition or instructions.

propositions.text: The jury requested further guidance, asking for the difference between manslaughter and second degree murder and a specific definition of manslaughter.
propositions.quote: the jurors evidently needed ― and expressly requested ― further guidance. They asked the judge to explain the difference between manslaughter and second degree murder, and to provide them with a “specific definition of manslaughter”.

paragraphs.summary: The jury expressly requested further guidance and a specific definition of manslaughter.

propositions.text: The judge concluded the jury was wrestling with the distinction but refused to give the requested definition or instructions on manslaughter elements.
propositions.quote: The judge concluded that the jury was having difficulty understanding the distinction... He nonetheless refused to give them the definition they had requested, or to provide them with any instructions as to the essential elements of manslaughter.

paragraphs.summary: The judge recognized jury difficulty but refused to provide the requested manslaughter definition or instructions.

propositions.text: No jury should be required to convict without understanding how elements of both offences relate to evidence.
propositions.quote: no 12 jurors should be required by a trial judge to convict the accused... without understanding how the elements of both might relate to the evidence before them

propositions.text: That is what happened here, which is improper.
propositions.quote: Yet that is what happened here.

paragraphs.summary: The dissent argues jurors must understand offence elements related to evidence, but here they were required to convict without that understanding.

propositions.text: The trial judge committed fatal error by not instructing on manslaughter elements; a new trial should be ordered.
propositions.quote: the trial judge thereby committed an error fatal to the jury’s verdict and that a new trial should be ordered for that reason.

paragraphs.summary: The dissent finds the trial judge's failure to instruct on manslaughter elements fatal and orders a new trial.

propositions.text: Trial judges must answer jury questions clearly, correctly and comprehensively, even if matter was reviewed in main charge.
propositions.quote: the paramount duty of trial judges to answer them “clearly, correctly and comprehensively”... “Even if the question relates to a matter that has been carefully reviewed in the main charge,”... “The jury must be given a full and proper response to their question. The jury is entitled to no less.”

paragraphs.summary: The law requires trial judges to answer jury questions clearly, correctly, and comprehensively, even if covered in the main charge.

propositions.text: The judge understood the jury needed further instructions on manslaughter but gave an unhelpful response instead of a simple instruction.
propositions.quote: the judge well understood the significance of the jury’s question... Their request could have been easily satisfied by a simple instruction... Instead, the jury received an unhelpful response.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the judge understood the jury's need for manslaughter instructions but gave an unhelpful response.

propositions.text: The trial judge's answer did little to explain the distinction and merely repeated parts of the charge the jury already had.
propositions.quote: The answer provided by the trial judge to the jury did little to explain the distinction... The judge then read selected portions of the charge, which the jury already had in its possession in written form.

propositions.text: The jury was entitled to know what legally constituted manslaughter to distinguish between offences.
propositions.quote: The jury was being asked to convict the appellant either of murder or manslaughter... The question was directed at a relevant and live issue and I can think of no good reason for depriving the jury of that instruction.

paragraphs.summary: The dissent argues the judge's answer was unhelpful and the jury was entitled to a clear legal definition of manslaughter.

propositions.text: The trial judge did not outline manslaughter elements fearing confusion and acquittal contrary to his direction.
propositions.quote: the trial judge opted not to outline the elements of manslaughter for two reasons: first, because to do so might increase the jury’s confusion... second, because the jury might... acquit the accused of manslaughter, contrary to his express direction

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge withheld manslaughter instructions fearing jury confusion and acquittal against his direction.

propositions.text: Withholding instructions denigrates the jury's role and presumes jurors cannot understand clear legal explanations.
propositions.quote: these rationales for withholding the requested assistance “denigrat[e] the role of the jury”... I reject the proposition that jurors can be confused, and deterred from doing their duty, by a clear explanation

propositions.text: The law presumes the jury's collective wisdom and intelligence and expects them to understand clear legal instructions.
propositions.quote: whose “collective wisdom and intelligence” the law should and does presume (R. v. Daley, 2007 SCC 53, [2007] 3 S.C.R. 523, at para. 139).

paragraphs.summary: The dissent rejects the judge's rationale, affirming the law presumes jurors' intelligence and ability to understand clear instructions.

propositions.text: The trial judge could have used model instructions from Watt’s Manual to satisfy the jury's request.
propositions.quote: the trial judge could easily have satisfied the jury’s request by adopting the model instructions for unlawful act manslaughter set out... in D. Watt, Watt’s Manual of Criminal Jury Instructions

paragraphs.summary: The dissent notes the judge could have used model instructions to explain manslaughter.

propositions.text: The jury was left without legal instruction on manslaughter and unable to accept that alternative in good conscience.
propositions.quote: the jury was left to reject the manslaughter alternative urged upon them by defence counsel without any instruction in law as to its constituent elements.

propositions.text: The jury requested but never received the assistance legally owed to them.
propositions.quote: Unwilling and unable to do so in good conscience, the jurors requested ― but never received ― the assistance of the trial judge to which they were by law entitled.

paragraphs.summary: The jury lacked legal instruction on manslaughter and did not receive the assistance they were entitled to.

propositions.text: Counsel's submissions do not remove the judge's duty to explain all offence elements and answer jury questions clearly.
propositions.quote: The submissions and concessions by counsel did not displace the judge’s obligation to explain the essential elements of every offence left open to the jury... and to answer the jury’s questions, if any, clearly and responsively.

propositions.text: That duty was not fulfilled here.
propositions.quote: That was not done here.

paragraphs.summary: The judge failed to fulfill the duty to explain offence elements and answer jury questions clearly despite counsel's submissions.

propositions.text: The jury needed to know what constituted each offence to make an informed decision between murder and manslaughter.
propositions.quote: The jury was entitled to make an informed decision through knowing beforehand what constituted each of the offences, so as to better distinguish between them.

propositions.text: The responsibility to instruct on relevant law lay with the trial judge and knowledge of manslaughter elements was material.
propositions.quote: The responsibility lay with the trial judge to instruct on relevant matters of law. It cannot be said... that knowledge of what constitutes manslaughter is not material.

paragraphs.summary: The dissent holds the judge had responsibility to instruct on manslaughter elements, which was material for the jury's decision.

propositions.text: The appeal is allowed and a new trial ordered due to the trial judge's failure to define manslaughter elements.
propositions.quote: I agree with O’Brien J.A. that the trial judge’s failure to define the elements of manslaughter amounted in itself to reversible error.

propositions.text: The jury should have been informed that manslaughter's mental element requires intentional force and objective foreseeability of bodily harm risk.
propositions.quote: the jury “should have been informed that the mental element of the offence... required both the intentional application of force... and the objective foreseeability of the risk of bodily harm

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees the trial judge erred by not defining manslaughter elements and orders a new trial.

propositions.text: Two aspects of the judge's charge are of particular concern.
propositions.quote: two aspects of the judge’s charge are of particular concern.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies two aspects of the judge's charge as particularly concerning.

propositions.text: The judge blurred the lines between murder and manslaughter by defining bodily harm for murder as any hurt interfering with health or comfort, more than brief or minor.
propositions.quote: the judge blurred the lines between murder and manslaughter by defining the bodily harm required for murder under s. 229 (a)(ii) ... as “any hurt or injury that interferes with health or comfort, and it has to be more than something that is just brief or fleeting or minor in nature”

propositions.text: O’Brien J.A. explains this bodily harm quality relates to manslaughter, not murder, possibly confusing the jury and diminishing intent required for murder.
propositions.quote: As O’Brien J.A. explains (at para. 86): This quality of bodily harm relates to the offence of manslaughter, not murder, and may have caused some confusion for the jury and caused the jury members to diminish the intent required to establish murder.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the judge blurred murder and manslaughter by misdefining bodily harm; O’Brien J.A. said this confused the jury and diminished murder intent.

propositions.text: The trial judge failed to highlight the defence's key point that appellant lacked subjective foresight due to intoxication, distinguishing murder from manslaughter.
propositions.quote: the trial judge failed to draw the jury’s attention to its most important component: that the appellant ... lacked the subjective foresight that distinguishes murder from manslaughter, as a matter of law.

propositions.text: The Crown acknowledges intoxication raising doubt about intent for murder was a main issue in the case.
propositions.quote: the Crown quite properly acknowledges in its factum, one of the main issues in the case was “whether intoxication raised a doubt about the intent for murder”

propositions.text: In pre-charge discussions, defence counsel agreed jury instruction should focus on intent and intoxication.
propositions.quote: in pre-charge discussions with the trial judge, “defence counsel agreed with the trial judge’s suggestio[n] that . . . the jury instruction should focus the jury on the real issues, intent and intoxication”

propositions.text: It is undisputed that a proper evidentiary basis for the intoxication submission was adduced at trial.
propositions.quote: It is undisputed that a proper evidentiary basis for this submission had been adduced at trial.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the judge failed to highlight defence's intoxication argument; the Crown agrees intoxication was a main issue; defence agreed jury focus on intent and intoxication; evidentiary basis undisputed.

propositions.text: The trial judge's invitation to the jury to ask further questions if unsatisfied with answers provides no comfort.
propositions.quote: I derive no comfort from the trial judge’s invitation to the jury to formulate a further question if his response to the questions they had already asked did not assist them

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no comfort in the trial judge's invitation to the jury to ask further questions if prior answers were unhelpful.

propositions.text: The jury had already asked about the distinction between offences in three ways; the judge said he responded as constrained by law.
propositions.quote: The jury had already formulated their sole concern ... in three different ways. The judge indicated ... he had responded ... “as constrained by the law”.

propositions.text: The judge's invitation could not reasonably encourage the jury to ask further questions on the same subject.
propositions.quote: the judge’s invitation could not reasonably have encouraged the jury to formulate further questions on the same subject.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the jury had asked about offence distinction multiple times; the judge responded constrained by law; invitation to ask more questions was unreasonable.

propositions.text: Jurors could not be expected to ask again for manslaughter definition or elements, and would likely get the same inadequate response.
propositions.quote: The jurors can hardly be expected to have later asked, once again, for a definition of manslaughter, or for its essential elements. And even if they had, they would presumably have received the response already given which ... was plainly inadequate.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds jurors unlikely to ask again for manslaughter definition and would receive the same inadequate response if they did.

propositions.text: The appeal is allowed, conviction quashed, and a new trial ordered.
propositions.quote: I would allow the appeal, quash the conviction, and order a new trial.

propositions.text: Appeal dismissed by McLachlin C.J. and Deschamps and Fish JJ. dissenting.
propositions.quote: Appeal dismissed, McLachlin C.J. and Deschamps and Fish JJ. dissenting.

propositions.text: Solicitors for appellant and respondent are named with locations.
propositions.quote: Solicitors for the appellant: O’Brien Devlin MacLeod, Calgary. Solicitor for the respondent: Attorney General of Alberta, Calgary.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal, quashes conviction, orders new trial; dissenting judges dismiss appeal; solicitors named.
